t: Sum of Scores of Built Strings — Z-Function to the Rescue
o: Because characters are prepended, s_i is simply the suffix of the final string s of length i, and its score is the length of the longest common prefix between that suffix and s itself. For s = "babab" the suffixes score 1, 0, 3, 0, 5, summing to 9; for "azbazbzaz" only lengths 2, 6 and 9 contribute, giving 2 + 3 + 9 = 14. So we must add up LCP(suffix starting at k, s) for every start position k from 0 to n-1. With n up to $10^5$ and strings like "aaaa...a", naive per-position comparison costs $O(n^2)$ in time and fails, which is exactly the situation the linear-time Z-function was designed for.
k: Prepending characters means each built string s_i is the length-i suffix of s, so all scores together are just the Z-array values of s (with z[0] = n).
The Z-function reuses matches inside the rightmost known match window [l, r], seeding z[i] with min(r - i, z[i - l]) before any character comparison.
Naive comparison degenerates to O(n^2) on periodic strings such as "aaaa", so a linear-time string structure is mandatory at n = 10^5.

a.n: Approach 1: Direct Comparison per Starting Position
a.i: For every start index k, walk forward counting how many characters match the beginning of s. This mirrors the definition of the score exactly and is trivially correct; on highly periodic inputs (e.g., all equal characters) each count can be O(n), making the total quadratic.
s: Initialize ans = n for the full-string suffix.
For each k from 1 to n-1, set cnt = 0.
While s[cnt] == s[k + cnt] and k + cnt < n, increment cnt.
Add cnt to ans and return ans.
a.t: O(n^2) worst case — e.g., s = "aaaa" makes every LCP scan linear.

a.i: Compute z[i] = LCP(s, s[i:]) using the classic amortized-linear algorithm: maintain [l, r], the farthest-reaching match segment found so far. If i lies inside it, position i - l already matched the same prefix there, so seed z[i] = min(r - i, z[i - l]); then extend by direct comparisons and widen the window when i + z[i] exceeds r. Each successful comparison pushes r forward, so total work is linear even on periodic strings.
s: Set z[0] = n and initialize l = r = 0.
For each i >= 1: if i < r, set z[i] = min(r - i, z[i - l]).
Extend z[i] by comparing s[z[i]] with s[i + z[i]] while they match.
If i + z[i] > r, update l = i and r = i + z[i].
Return the sum of all z[i].
a.t: O(n) — r never moves backward, so extension steps are amortized O(1) per index.
a.sp: O(n) — the z-array of size n.

w: Recognizing that the scores are exactly the Z-array is the whole problem; say so explicitly, implement Approach 2, and fall back to hashing + binary search (O(n log n)) if Z-function details slip your mind. Pitfalls: forgetting z[0] = n (the full string always matches itself), seeding without the min cap against r - i (breaks correctness), and overflowing 32 bits when summing since the answer can reach about n(n+1)/2 ~ 5 * 10^9. Related follow-ups: number of occurrences of each prefix (KMP), or minimum characters to append to make a palindrome, both reuse the same structures.
